Doing so does not mean forgetting or excusing past wrongs; it means recognizing that violence begets cycles of harm that ultimately undermine the very justice that survivors deserve.

The Moral Insufficiency of Retribution

At the heart of the anti-retaliation position lies a philosophical distinction between justice and revenge. Justice, in the classical sense articulated by thinkers from Aristotle to Immanuel Kant, requires proportionality, impartiality, and the application of generalizable principles. Revenge, by contrast, is personal, often disproportionate, and driven by emotional satisfaction rather than moral reasoning. When an individual takes violent revenge against a former oppressor, the act may deliver momentary satisfaction, but it does not necessarily advance justice. A former torturer who becomes the victim of violent reprisal has not been judged, sentenced, or held accountable through any process that society can recognize as legitimate. The act simply reverses the direction of harm without establishing any higher moral order.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt, reflecting on the aftermath of totalitarianism, warned against the dangers of conflating vengeance with justice. Arendt argued that the desire for revenge, while entirely human, belongs to the realm of nature—the predictable responses of injured parties—rather than the realm of politics, which demands reason, deliberation, and the pursuit of common goods. If a post-dictatorship society permits or encourages individuals to act on vengeance alone, it essentially abandons the political project of building a just society and descends into a state where power belongs to whoever is willing to use the most force. This is precisely the logic that sustained the dictatorship in the first place.

Moreover, retribution as a basis for violence fails to account for the complexity of complicity. Under a dictatorship, individuals occupy a wide spectrum: from enthusiastic perpetrators to reluctant cooperators, from informants acting under duress to bystanders who chose silence. A system of individualized violence lacks the capacity—and the moral authority—to distinguish among these categories. The result is inevitably arbitrary: some who bear significant responsibility escape harm, while others who played marginal roles suffer devastating consequences. Arbitrary violence is not justice; it is merely a new form of injustice dressed in the language of righteousness.

The Perpetuation of Cycles of Violence

One of the most empirically grounded arguments against post-dictatorship violence is the well-documented pattern of cyclical conflict. History demonstrates repeatedly that societies which permit or encourage retaliatory violence after a regime change frequently find themselves trapped in prolonged instability. The aftermath of the French Revolution, the sectarian violence following state collapse in the Middle East, and the cycles of ethnic retribution in post-colonial Africa all illustrate how initial acts of vengeance can escalate into broader conflicts that consume entire generations.

The mechanism behind this cycle is both psychological and structural. Psychologically, violence is traumatizing not only to its victims but to its perpetrators. Individuals who commit violent acts often experience lasting psychological damage, which impairs their ability to function as contributing members of a peaceful society. Structurally, acts of private or semi-organized violence undermine the authority of emerging institutions, erode the rule of law, and create incentives for other groups to arm themselves in self-defense or to launch preemptive attacks. Each act of retribution produces new grievances, new perceived injustices, and new motivations for further violence.

South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, despite its imperfections, remains an instructive example. The architects of the post-apartheid transition—including Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu—recognized that a full accounting of apartheid crimes through retributive violence would have been impossible without fracturing the nation. The choice was not between justice and impunity but between different models of justice. The restorative model, centered on testimony, acknowledgment, and conditional amnesty, acknowledged the reality of wrongs while deliberately breaking the cycle. Not every society must follow this exact template, but the underlying principle—that violence perpetuates harm rather than resolving it—holds broad applicability.

The Erosion of Institutional Legitimacy

Perhaps the most consequential danger of permitting individuals to use violence against former oppressors is the damage it inflicts on the fledgling institutions that a post-dictatorship society desperately needs. The rule of law—the foundation upon which democratic governance rests—requires that the state hold a legitimate monopoly on the use of force. This monopoly exists not for the state's benefit but for the protection of all citizens: individuals who might otherwise seek violent resolution are disincentivized from doing so, knowing that disputes will be adjudicated through courts, mediated through law, and enforced through accountable institutions.

When individuals take violence into their own hands, they implicitly declare that these institutions are not sufficient, are not to be trusted, or do not exist within any meaningful timeframe. In the immediate aftermath of a dictatorship, institutions are fragile, under-resourced, and often distrusted—precisely because they were instruments of oppression. Allowing retaliatory violence at this critical juncture sends the message that personal power, not institutional processes, is the true currency of society. This message undermines the very long-term project of building institutions strong enough to prevent the return of authoritarianism.

International human rights law reinforces this point. The right to life, the prohibition of torture, and the right to a fair trial are not luxuries to be dispensed with in times of emotional urgency; they are foundational protections that exist precisely because history has shown that the state and individuals alike cannot be trusted to exercise power over others without accountability. When individuals commit violence against former oppressors, they assume powers that no person or group should possess: the power to judge, sentence, and execute without due process. No grievance—however severe—can morally authorize such an assumption of absolute power.

Critics of the anti-violence position often argue that it is an exercise in privilege—that those who have not suffered dictatorship have no right to tell survivors to remain peaceful. This objection has emotional force but does not withstand scrutiny. The argument against retaliatory violence is not a dismissal of suffering; it is a recognition that suffering does not transform immoral acts into moral ones. Violence committed by the victim against the former oppressor is no less violent, no less destructive, and no less corrosive to human dignity than violence committed by the oppressor in the first place.

What the anti-violence position demands is not that victims suffer in silence but that they find means of pursuing justice that do not replicate the very harms they have endured. This is an extraordinarily difficult ask, and no advocate of nonviolence should minimize the emotional weight of that demand. But the alternative—a society in which every aggrieved individual is entitled to mete out punishment according to their own sense of proportionality—is not a society that anyone, including those who have suffered, would wish to inhabit.

Conclusion

The fall of a dictatorship creates an unprecedented opportunity for a society to choose a new path. Retribution may feel like justice, but it is justice's shadow. It offers the appearance of accountability without its substance, the satisfaction of punishment without the legitimacy of law, and the catharsis of violence without the permanence of healing. Individuals do not have a right to use violence against former oppressors because violence, by its nature, cannot be a sufficient cause for the pursuit of justice. It is disproportionate, arbitrary, cyclical, and corrosive to the institutions that a free society requires. The path beyond dictatorship is arduous, but it lies in the painstaking work of building legal systems, truth-seeking processes, and civic culture—not in exchanging one era of violence for another.

The Case Against Retributive Violence in Post-Authoritarian Transitions

Introduction

When a dictatorship collapses, the streets fill with people who have buried children, lost years to prisons, and watched neighbors disappear. The impulse toward vengeance in such moments is not merely understandable—it is arguably the most natural human response to profound injustice. Yet the moral case against acting on that impulse remains compelling. Individuals do not possess a right to inflict violence upon former oppressors for the sake of retribution alone, because retribution, however emotionally satisfying, cannot bear the moral weight required to justify taking human life or inflicting suffering. This essay argues that private retributive violence in transitional contexts fails on grounds of moral principle, epistemic reliability, political consequence, and the very logic of justice that its advocates invoke.

The Distinction Between Justice and Vengeance

The strongest argument for post-dictatorial violence rests on a conflation of two distinct concepts: justice and vengeance. Justice is a public good, characterized by impartiality, proportionality, and procedure. Vengeance is a private satisfaction, characterized by the injured party's own assessment of what is owed. The former requires that the punisher be disinterested; the latter demands precisely the opposite.

This distinction is not mere semantics. When a victim's family executes a former secret police officer, the act may resemble punishment in form, but it lacks the features that make punishment legitimate rather than merely another instance of violence. There is no determination of guilt by anyone other than the aggrieved. There is no calibration of penalty to offense beyond the intensity of grief. There is no possibility of error correction. What remains is the raw exercise of power by whoever currently holds it—which is, notably, the defining characteristic of the dictatorship that has just fallen.

The philosopher's question here is unavoidable: if the right to inflict violence derives from having been wronged, what limits that right? The victim who was tortured claims the right to torture. The victim whose mother was killed claims the right to kill mothers. Retribution offers no internal principle of restraint, because its measure is subjective harm rather than objective desert. Any account of justified violence must contain such a principle, or it collapses into the assertion that suffering entitles one to inflict suffering—a proposition that would equally have justified the oppressor's original acts had he claimed grievance, as oppressors invariably do.

The Epistemic Problem

Authoritarian regimes function precisely by obscuring responsibility. They rely on compartmentalized bureaucracies, coerced informants, ambiguous chains of command, and the widespread complicity of ordinary people who signed documents, taught propaganda, or simply looked away. This structure makes accurate individual attribution of guilt extraordinarily difficult—and it is exactly this difficulty that private violence is least equipped to handle.

The historical record is unambiguous. In the French épuration following liberation, thousands were killed in extrajudicial reprisals; subsequent investigation revealed that a substantial portion of victims were guilty of nothing beyond personal enmity with their accusers, or of ambiguous survival choices under occupation. In post-1945 Eastern Europe, accusations of collaboration became instruments for settling property disputes and ethnic grievances. In Iraq after 2003, de-Ba'athification and the violence accompanying it swept up schoolteachers and engineers whose party membership had been a condition of employment.

The epistemic problem is not merely that mistakes occur. It is that private retributive violence systematically selects for the wrong targets. The accessible are punished while the powerful escape: the low-level prison guard is lynched while the minister who designed the prison system flees abroad with resources intact. Those with local enemies are denounced; those with local allies are protected. Violence distributed according to accessibility and social position is not justice under any description—it is a lottery weighted toward the vulnerable.

The Political Consequences

Even granting, for argument's sake, that some individuals genuinely deserve violent punishment, the question of who may administer it and under what circumstances is a political question with foreseeable consequences.

A transitional society faces a fundamental task: establishing that the state, and only the state acting through law, may legitimately use force. Every act of private retributive violence undermines this project directly. It teaches the population that political disputes are settled by whoever can mobilize violence, and it teaches the remnants of the old regime that surrender means death—thereby giving them every incentive to fight rather than negotiate a transition.

This latter point deserves emphasis, because it is frequently dismissed as mere pragmatism unworthy of moral consideration. It is not. If the credible threat of retributive violence extends the life of a dictatorship by years, then the choice to embrace such violence is a choice to accept additional years of oppression—additional torture, additional disappearances, additional dead. The moral cost is not hypothetical. Spain's transition, whatever its serious deficiencies regarding historical memory, involved no mass reprisals and no return to civil war. Chile's negotiated transition, constrained and unsatisfying as it was, eventually produced trials of Pinochet-era officials that would have been impossible had the military faced immediate extrajudicial killing. Retributive violence purchases immediate satisfaction with future suffering, and the future suffering falls disproportionately on people who did not choose the transaction.

There is a further consequence. Cycles of retributive violence are notoriously self-sustaining. The families of those killed in reprisals acquire their own grievances, which they experience with the same intensity and justify with the same logic. Yugoslavia's dissolution demonstrated how effectively memories of 1940s reprisals could be mobilized fifty years later. A society that licenses private vengeance does not resolve its conflicts; it schedules them.

The Insufficiency of Retribution as a Justification

The core claim of this essay is narrow but important: retribution alone cannot justify violence. This is not a claim that violence is never justified. Self-defense justifies violence, because it prevents imminent harm. The defense of others justifies violence on the same grounds. Resistance against an ongoing tyranny may be justified because it aims at ending present oppression. Even certain forms of preventive action may be justified where a former regime retains the capacity and intent to return to power.

What these justifications share is that they are forward-looking. They point to harm prevented, not harm avenged. Retribution, by contrast, is purely backward-looking. It aims at no future good; it seeks to balance a moral ledger by adding suffering to the world. And here the burden of proof falls heavily on its advocates. Violence involves the deliberate destruction of a human being's life, body, or capacity to flourish. To justify such an act requires showing that something of comparable weight is achieved. Prevention of future killing meets this standard. The satisfaction of a moral intuition about desert does not obviously do so.

Consider the structure of the retributivist claim carefully. It asserts that the world is better—or at least more just—when a wrongdoer suffers, independent of any consequence that suffering produces. But this is a substantive metaphysical claim, and one that many thoughtful people reject. It is not the kind of claim that can bear the weight of authorizing private citizens to kill. Where a moral principle is genuinely contested, and where acting on it involves irreversible harm, restraint is the appropriate response.

Moreover, retribution's advocates typically smuggle in forward-looking considerations while claiming to rely on desert alone. They argue that punishment vindicates victims, affirms their dignity, or expresses society's condemnation. These are real goods—but they are goods that formal legal processes deliver far better than private violence. A trial that establishes facts on the public record, names crimes, and imposes an authorized penalty vindicates victims in a way that a body in a ditch cannot. The expressive function of punishment requires an authoritative speaker; a lynch mob speaks for no one but itself.

Objections Considered

The objection from impunity. Critics will argue that in many transitions, formal justice simply does not arrive. Amnesty laws are passed, courts are captured by regime holdovers, and torturers retire on state pensions. In such circumstances, is not private violence the only justice available?

The force of this objection must be acknowledged: impunity is a genuine injustice, and the frustration it generates is legitimate. But the argument does not follow. That formal justice has failed does not establish that private violence succeeds; it may simply mean that justice is unavailable, which is a tragedy rather than a permission. And the practical claim is doubtful. Impunity is most effectively contested through the accumulation of documentation, the maintenance of political pressure, the pursuit of universal jurisdiction abroad, and the patient work of civil society—strategies that private violence actively undermines by discrediting victims' movements and providing pretexts for repression. Argentina's Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo achieved the reversal of amnesty laws and the imprisonment of junta leaders through decades of nonviolent persistence. This was slower than vengeance. It was also more complete.

The objection from victim standing. Some argue that outsiders lack standing to counsel restraint to those who have suffered. This has rhetorical power but limited logical force. The question of what is morally permissible does not depend on the identity of the person asking, and the interests at stake extend beyond any individual victim—to the wrongly accused, to future generations, and to the society that must be rebuilt. Victims possess unique moral authority to speak about their suffering. They do not thereby acquire authority over the lives of others.

The objection from deterrence. Might not visible reprisals deter future dictators? The historical evidence suggests otherwise. Dictators are deterred by the prospect of trial and lasting disgrace far more than by the possibility of chaotic violence they may hope to escape or exploit. Indeed, the anticipation of vengeance more often persuades authoritarians to hold power tighter.

Conclusion

The argument advanced here is not that former oppressors should escape consequence, nor that victims should forgive, nor that the demand for accountability is misplaced. It is that accountability must be public, procedural, and forward-looking to be justified—and that retribution stripped of these features amounts to violence in search of a rationale.

The deepest reason to refuse retributive violence is that it accepts the moral framework of the dictatorship. Authoritarian regimes operate on the premise that those with power may dispose of those without it according to their own judgment, and that suffering inflicted on enemies requires no justification beyond their status as enemies. To adopt this premise in victory is to preserve the regime's most important legacy while destroying only its personnel.

A society emerging from tyranny faces a choice about what kind of society it will be. The choice is made not in constitutional conventions but in the moments when a former torturer is recognized in a market square and the crowd must decide what it is. Choosing restraint in that moment is not weakness, and it is not forgiveness. It is the assertion that something has genuinely changed—that here, now, violence requires a justification, and the fact that a man deserves to suffer is not enough.

The Moral and Pragmatic Limits of Retribution: Why Individuals Should Not Resort to Violence in Seeking Justice After a Dictatorship

1. Introduction

When a long‑standing dictatorship collapses, the collective yearning for justice can become palpable. Years of authoritarian rule leave deep scars—political repression, disappearances, torture, and economic predation. In the vacuum that follows, former victims and their allies often feel an acute desire to “settle the score” with those who orchestrated the regime’s abuses. Yet the impulse to use personal or vigilante violence as a means of retribution raises profound ethical, legal, and practical concerns. This essay argues that, once a dictatorship falls, individuals do not possess a legitimate right to employ violence in the name of justice. The rationale rests on three interlocking pillars: the primacy of the rule of law, the moral insufficiency of retribution alone, and the pragmatic imperative to prevent cycles of revenge that could destabilise nascent democracies.

2. Justice as an Institutional Enterprise

2.1 The Meaning of Justice in Post‑Authoritarian Societies

Justice, in political philosophy, is commonly understood as the fair allocation of rights, responsibilities, and consequences within a community. When a state has been the principal violator of those rights, the re‑establishment of a legitimate public order becomes a precondition for any meaningful justice. This involves:

  • Due process: The guarantee that accused persons are tried by competent, impartial tribunals.
  • Transparency: Public access to evidence and proceedings, allowing society to witness accountability.
  • Consistency: The application of the same legal standards to all citizens, including former rulers.

Only institutions endowed with democratic legitimacy can satisfy these criteria. Individuals, acting on personal grievance, lack the authority to mete out punishment that meets these standards.

2.2 The “Right” to Justice Versus the “Right” to Violence

The right to seek justice is a universally recognised human right (Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 8). However, that right does not extend to a licence for self‑help violence. International human‑rights law consistently affirms that the monopoly on the legitimate use of force rests with the state, which must exercise it within a framework of law. Private violence, regardless of its motivation, violates the principle of state sovereignty over the use of force and can be classified as criminal assault or murder.

3. The Moral Insufficiency of Retribution

3.1 Retribution as a Moral Principle

Retributive justice holds that punishment is justified because the offender deserves it. Yet moral philosophers have long debated whether retribution alone can justify the deliberate infliction of harm. Immanuel Kant famously argued that moral deserts are necessary, but even he insisted that the mode of punishment must be proportionate and lawful. When individuals take the law into their own hands, proportionality is impossible to gauge: the aggrieved party’s emotional state and personal vendetta can inflate the scale of violence far beyond any principled measure.

3.2 The Problem of Subjectivity

Retribution is inherently subjective. What feels like “justice” to a former victim may be perceived as disproportionate vengeance by a neutral observer. In post‑dictatorship contexts, personal trauma, cultural narratives, and collective memory intersect, often producing divergent expectations of what constitutes a fitting punishment. Without an objective, procedural mechanism, the risk of arbitrary, excessive, or discriminatory violence is high.

3.3 The Moral Imperative of Non‑Maleficence

A core tenet of moral philosophy, the principle of non‑maleficence (“do no harm”) obliges us to minimise unnecessary suffering. While victims have a legitimate claim to acknowledgement and reparation, the additional harm inflicted by private violence—including the trauma to the perpetrator, the victim’s family, and the broader community—cannot be justified merely by the desire for revenge. The moral weight of preventing further suffering often outweighs the claim to retaliatory justice.

4. Pragmatic Considerations: Preventing the Cycle of Violence

4.1 Historical Precedents

History offers cautionary tales. In the aftermath of the Spanish Civil War, the “represión” (repression) by both Franco’s regime and later the “paseíllo” (revenge killings) by Republicans produced long‑term social fragmentation. Similarly, post‑Saddam Iraq saw a proliferation of sectarian revenge attacks that exacerbated civil war dynamics rather than delivering justice. In each case, the absence of credible state institutions transformed personal grievances into inter‑generational cycles of violence.

Conversely, societies that opted for institutional accountability—e.g., the German Strafjustiz after 1945, the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), and the Argentine Juicios por la Verdad—demonstrated that peaceful, legal mechanisms can foster societal reconciliation without resorting to vigilante retribution.

4.2 Stability and the Rule of Law

A nascent democracy is fragile; the first test of its legitimacy is its capacity to enforce law without resorting to extrajudicial violence. When individuals assume the right to punish, they undermine the state’s monopoly on force, eroding the very foundation needed for lasting peace. The resulting lawlessness can be exploited by residual authoritarian actors, militarised groups, or opportunistic elites, all of whom may use the chaos to reassert power.

4.3 Economic and Social Reconstruction

Post‑conflict reconstruction requires social cohesion. Private revenge killings fracture community trust, deter investment, and generate an environment of fear. By contrast, state‑led accountability—including trials, reparations, and memorialisation—has been shown to rebuild social capital and stimulate post‑conflict recovery, as illustrated by the economic resurgence in post‑authoritarian Spain after the Transición.

5. Transitional Justice as an Alternative Path

5.1 Components of a Comprehensive Strategy

  1. Truth‑Seeking: Commissions that document abuses, provide a public record, and honour victims’ testimonies.
  2. Prosecutorial Accountability: Trials conducted under international standards, guaranteeing due process and the right to a defence.
  3. Reparations: Monetary, symbolic, or institutional补偿, addressing material and psychological harms.
  4. Institutional Reform: Dismantling repressive structures, vetting security forces, and establishing independent judiciaries.
  5. Memorialisation: Public remembrance that educates future generations and reinforces a collective commitment to non‑recurrence.

5.2 Why These Mechanisms Trump Personal Violence

Each of the above mechanisms addresses the core demands of justice: acknowledgement, accountability, and restitution. Crucially, they do so within a legal framework that respects the rights of both victims and perpetrators, thereby legitimising the new democratic order. By contrast, personal vengeance offers only a transient emotional release, leaving systemic injustices intact.

6. The Ethical Responsibility of Individuals

While individuals should be empowered to demand accountability, the moral responsibility lies in channeling that demand through lawful avenues:

  • Civic Engagement: Participation in peaceful protests, advocacy for legal reforms, and support for human‑rights organisations.
  • Witness Testimony: Providing evidence to truth commissions or courts, thereby contributing to the judicial record.
  • Collective Memory: Engaging in public education and commemoration to ensure that the past is not erased.

In this way, individuals fulfill a positive duty to justice without assuming the negative right to harm others.

7. Conclusion

When a dictatorship falls, the desire for retribution is understandable, rooted in deep personal and collective wounds. Yet retribution alone cannot legitimise violence. Justice, in a civilised society, must be institutional, proportional, and transparent. Individuals may—indeed must—pursue justice, but they must do so through the rule of law, transitional justice mechanisms, and civic activism. By refusing to grant themselves the right to extrajudicial violence, former victims and their societies can lay the groundwork for a durable peace, a functioning democracy, and a moral order that does not replicate the very oppression it seeks to rectify. Only then can the promise of true justice replace the fleeting satisfaction of revenge.

The Imperative of Restraint: Why Justice Cannot Be Forged Through Violence in Post-Dictatorship Societies

The collapse of a dictatorship unleashes powerful currents of grief, anger, and desire for retribution among a populace long subjected to systematic oppression. When the machinery of state terror is finally dismantled, survivors and victims' families face the haunting presence of former oppressors—bureaucrats, military officials, paramilitaries, and collaborators who inflicted immeasurable suffering. The instinct to strike back, to exact revenge through the same violent means that were visited upon the innocent, is profoundly human and emotionally comprehensible. Yet however understandable this impulse may be, individuals possess no inherent right to use violence against former oppressors, and retribution alone—however justified by past horrors—cannot serve as a sufficient moral or legal basis for violent action. The establishment of a just and stable post-authoritarian order demands that societies resist the seductive simplicity of vengeance and instead embrace the more arduous path of institutional justice. This principle is not rooted in forgiveness for unforgivable acts or in forgetting crimes that must be remembered; rather, it derives from the recognition that violence as retribution corrodes the very foundations of the democracy that oppressed peoples have sacrificed so much to build.

The foremost argument against individual violent retribution lies in the paramount necessity of reestablishing the rule of law. Dictatorships thrive by destroying legal frameworks, replacing impartial justice with arbitrary terror, and conflating state power with the whims of the powerful. The transition to democracy represents an opportunity—indeed, an obligation—to reconstruct a system where laws, not individuals, determine guilt and punishment. When citizens take justice into their own hands through violence, they replicate the lawlessness of the regime they overthrew. They replace one arbitrary exercise of power with another, signaling that might, rather than right, continues to govern society. Legal philosopher H.L.A. Hart argued that rules of recognition, adjudication, and change form the core of a functioning legal system. Vigilante violence obliterates these rules, instituting instead a retroactive, personalized form of punishment that undermines the predictability and fairness essential to legitimate governance. If a society cannot restrain its own victims from violence, how can it claim moral superiority over the unrestrained violence of its former oppressors? The rule of law must be universal or it is merely another tool of power.

Beyond institutional concerns, the moral philosophy surrounding retribution reveals its inadequacy as a justification for violence. Retributive justice, in its purest form, rests on the principle of "just deserts"—that wrongdoers should suffer in proportion to their crimes. Yet when individuals enact this principle through force, they collapse the critical distinction between justice and vengeance. Vengeance is emotional, personal, and unlimited; it seeks satisfaction rather than proportionality. More dangerously, retributive violence initiates cycles of bloodshed that can perpetuate across generations. The children of those killed in extrajudicial purges become tomorrow's avengers, transforming political transitions into feuds. Historical evidence demonstrates this pattern repeatedly: the French Revolution's Reign of Terror devoured its own architects; post-colonial purges in various nations replaced one form of violence with another, delaying genuine democratic consolidation. When societies legitimize violence based on past suffering alone, they authorize an endless backward-looking calculus of grievance that makes peace impossible. The harm done by oppressors, however monstrous, cannot retroactively grant moral license to their victims to become victimizers. As Hannah Arendt warned, the danger of violence is that it can "destroy power" but never create it, leaving societies anarchic rather than free.

The practical consequences of widespread retributive violence further expose its indefensibility as a basis for post-dictatorship transition. Societies emerging from authoritarianism are profoundly fragile, their social fabrics torn by years of division, suspicion, and trauma. Violence against former oppressors—whether they be high-ranking officials or low-level collaborators—deepens these fractures rather than healing them. It creates climate of fear among entire categories of people, including those who may have been coerced into complicity or seek genuine redemption. This atmosphere of intimidation prevents national reconciliation, a process that, while difficult and imperfect, remains essential for long-term stability. Moreover, violent purges often target the wrong individuals or disproportionately affect marginal groups, lacking the evidentiary standards and procedural safeguards necessary for accurate accountability. Without due process, societies risk punishing the guilty insufficiently while devastating the innocent who were merely associated with the old regime. The instability created by such violence can even provide pretexts for military intervention or the reassertion of authoritarian control, as security forces claim necessity in quelling "chaos"—a tragic irony where the pursuit of justice becomes the weapon for resurrecting tyranny.

Critics of this position might argue that institutional processes are too slow, too lenient, or vulnerable to manipulation by remnants of the old regime. They point correctly to the profound psychological need of victims for visible, tangible justice and the legitimate fear that without immediate consequences, oppressors will regroup and reclaim power. These concerns are not trivial. However, they conflate the urgency of accountability with the method of achieving it. The answer to institutional weakness is not to abandon institutions but to strengthen them through robust transitional justice mechanisms: international tribunals, hybrid courts, truth and reconciliation commissions, and lustration laws. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, however imperfect, demonstrated that public acknowledgment and accountability could be achieved without executions or widespread violence. Conversely, the violent purges following the 1979 Iranian Revolution produced not justice but a new authoritarianism that itself became a perpetrator of mass violence, illustrating how retributive violence begets more oppression. Institutional justice, while slower, creates precedents, establishes historical records, and builds civic trust—none of which individual violence can accomplish.

Prompt:
Write an essay arguing in favor of the stance that individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls, emphasizing that retribution alone is not a sufficient cause for violence.
Model Response:

When a dictatorship collapses, societies often stand at a crossroads between the desire for justice and the temptation of revenge. The wounds inflicted by oppression—torture, disappearances, censorship, economic plunder, humiliation—are real and deep. Yet even in the face of those wounds, individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors. The mere fact of past harm, and the desire for retribution against those who caused it, is not a sufficient cause to authorize private violence.

This is not a claim that oppressors should go unpunished or that victims must “move on” without redress. Rather, it is a claim about the limits of individual entitlement to resort to violence, and about what kind of justice can actually sustain a decent political order after tyranny.

Several interconnected arguments support this stance: the primacy of the rule of law and human rights norms; the danger of cycles of revenge and collective punishment; the moral distinction between justice and retribution; the importance of shared institutions for assigning responsibility; and the availability of nonviolent methods of accountability and repair.

1. The rule of law prohibits private violence, even in response to grave injustice

At the heart of any just political order is the idea that the use of force is regulated by law and, as far as possible, monopolized by legitimate public authorities. This is the core of the rule of law: disputes are resolved and wrongs are addressed through public procedures, not through private acts of vengeance.

If individuals were granted a right to use violence against former oppressors, that would effectively abandon this principle at precisely the moment when it is most needed. After dictatorship, societies are trying to move from a system where power and violence were arbitrary, to one where they are constrained by law. Allowing private violent retribution, even in the name of “justice,” would leave the old logic of arbitrary force intact under a new label.

Moreover, human rights norms—which are often invoked to condemn dictatorships—also limit how even legitimate states may treat wrongdoers. Torture, extrajudicial killing, and cruel or degrading punishment are prohibited. If we argue that former victims have a “right” to violate those norms in the name of justice, we implicitly treat human rights as negotiable: binding when condemning dictators, but dispensable when punishing them. That double standard erodes the very moral framework that made the dictatorship condemnable in the first place.

To put it plainly: if the wrongness of dictatorship lies partly in its lawless and violent treatment of individuals, we cannot remedy that wrong by authorizing lawless and violent treatment in return.

2. Private violence produces cycles of revenge, not stable justice

Retributive violence rarely stays confined to the “guilty.” Once individuals assume the right to harm former oppressors, several problems arise:

  • Attribution becomes contested. Who counts as an oppressor? Only the dictator and his closest enforcers? Lower-level officials? Party members? Citizens who collaborated under duress? Once individuals themselves are deciding who “deserves” to be hurt, lines blur and the circle of targets expands.

  • Perceptions of injustice are reciprocal. Those who supported or served the dictatorship often see themselves as having had reasons—fear, ideology, economic survival. When they or their families are attacked, they see themselves as victims of injustice and seek retaliation. Violence breeds counterviolence.

  • Collective identities get weaponized. Oppressors and victims frequently map onto ethnic, religious, or class divisions. Private revenge easily becomes collective: “they did this to us; now we must do it to them.” Entire communities can be marked as fair game on the basis of shared identity rather than individual responsibility.

Historical experience supports this. Post-authoritarian settings where private retribution has been tacitly tolerated—whether in parts of the Balkans, some Latin American transitions, or local score-settling after wars—tend to see spirals of vendetta, settling of unrelated personal feuds under the cover of “justice,” and long-term instability.

If the aim is to prevent future oppression and build a peaceful order, then endorsing a right to private violence is self-defeating. It cultivates habits of vengeance instead of habits of lawfulness.

3. Justice is more than the satisfaction of retributive emotion

Anger, resentment, and a desire for the suffering of egregious wrongdoers are understandable human reactions to oppression. Many moral traditions even acknowledge a limited place for retribution within justice: the idea that it is fitting for a wrongdoer to be held to account in a way that reflects the seriousness of the wrong.

But “retribution” in the sense of pure payback—hurting those who hurt you, because they hurt you—is morally insufficient as a justification for violence. Several distinctions matter here:

  • Retribution vs. protection. Punishment can be justified in part by the need to protect society, deter future abuses, and affirm shared values. Violence motivated purely by “they harmed us; now we will harm them” contributes nothing to protection or deterrence when performed outside any institutional framework.

  • Retribution vs. recognition of wrong. Justice involves publicly recognizing the wrong that occurred, the dignity of victims, and the responsibility of perpetrators. This is best done through procedures that investigate, deliberate, and record the truth. Private violence makes no public argument; it neither explains nor justifies itself beyond a sentiment of anger.

  • Retribution vs. proportionality. Even when punishment is deserved, moral constraints of proportionality apply: responses must be measured and targeted. Private vengeance, especially when fueled by trauma, easily exceeds any proportionate response.

The fact that someone “deserves” to suffer—if they do—does not give any particular individual the right to inflict that suffering. We recognize this in ordinary criminal law: a victim of theft, however furious, is not entitled to beat the thief. To treat retributive emotion as sufficient grounds for violence is to dissolve the boundary between justice and raw vengeance.

4. Assigning guilt is complex; individuals are not equipped to act as judge, jury, and executioner

Dictatorships and oppressive systems are rarely sustained by a handful of obviously monstrous individuals. They are systemic, involving:

  • leaders who give orders
  • security forces and bureaucrats who implement policies
  • judges who enforce unjust laws
  • businessmen who profit
  • neighbors who inform on neighbors
  • bystanders who look away

Sorting out degrees of responsibility is difficult. It requires evidence, contextual understanding, consideration of coercion, levels of authority, and institutional roles. Formal processes—trials, commissions, lustration procedures—are imperfect but are designed to handle exactly these questions.

If individuals claim a right to use violence against “former oppressors,” they necessarily assume they can single-handedly determine:

  1. Who counts as an oppressor,
  2. What level of punishment is appropriate,
  3. How to deal with mitigating factors (coercion, ignorance, remorse),
  4. Whether the person still poses a threat.

They are, in effect, claiming a right to be judge, jury, and executioner in their own case. That is precisely what rule-of-law systems are designed to prevent, because human judgment is fallible, biased, and prone to overreach—especially when traumatized.

Justice after dictatorship demands careful moral and factual distinctions; private violence erases those distinctions.

5. The transition away from oppression requires breaking with its methods

A dictatorship is not just defined by who holds power; it is defined by the norms that structure political life. Under authoritarian rule, violence often functions as:

  • a tool of political control,
  • a language of social relations,
  • a way to settle disputes and enforce obedience outside any genuine legal framework.

If, after the fall of the dictatorship, citizens instead adopt the same language and methods—violence, intimidation, fear—it signals continuity with oppression, not a break from it. The message becomes: “We have changed the targets, but not the tools.”

A stable, just order requires replacing the regime’s methods with new norms:

  • public justification instead of secret orders,
  • trials instead of disappearances,
  • imprisonment or other lawful penalties instead of lynching,
  • truth-telling instead of enforced silence.

Denying a right to private violence in the name of justice is not a concession to former oppressors; it is a commitment to a different kind of politics, one in which no one is above the law—including the victims when they are tempted to become avengers.

6. Nonviolent mechanisms for justice exist—and are morally preferable

The rejection of a right to violent retribution does not entail passivity or forgetfulness. It leaves open, and indeed encourages, a range of nonviolent approaches:

  • Criminal trials for major perpetrators. These can be domestic, hybrid, or international. Their legitimacy comes from being public, evidence-based, and constrained by procedural rights.

  • Truth and reconciliation commissions. These can establish a record of abuses, validate victims’ experiences, and recommend reforms and reparations.

  • Lustration and vetting. Excluding key perpetrators from public office or positions of power can reduce future risk without resorting to violence.

  • Reparations and restitution. Material and symbolic compensation can help recognize the harm suffered and support reconstruction of lives.

  • Institutional reforms. Reforming the police, judiciary, military, and security services addresses the structural conditions that enabled oppression.

None of these mechanisms is perfect or free of politics, but they embody a different ethic: they treat justice as a public, reason-guided enterprise, rather than a private matter of inflicting pain.

If relatively effective nonviolent paths to justice are available, the claim that individuals have a right to use violence for retribution loses even further plausibility. Rights to violent self-help are sometimes defended, if at all, in conditions of complete lawlessness and necessity. But transitional justice, by definition, is about building institutions; the existence of such institutions undercuts any moral claim to bypass them through private force.

7. Moral symmetry: refusing to mirror the oppressor

Finally, there is a moral reason related to symmetry. Oppressive regimes typically:

  • deny the moral equality of their victims,
  • treat them as obstacles, tools, or threats,
  • assume they may be harmed without due process.

When victims later claim a right to violently harm former oppressors outside legal channels, they risk reproducing the same underlying moral posture: that some people’s rights are suspended because they are “the enemy” or “deserve it.”

To refuse private violence is to affirm that even those who have done terrible wrongs remain bearers of certain basic rights—not because they are sympathetic, but because human rights do not vanish when they are inconvenient. Upholding that standard is difficult and emotionally taxing; it can feel like an injustice in itself. Yet it is precisely this discipline that distinguishes a moral order from a retaliatory one.

Conclusion

In the immediate aftermath of dictatorship, the urge to use violence against former oppressors is understandable. The suffering they caused is real, and the desire to see them hurt can be intense. But this desire, however human, does not translate into a right.

Individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors, because:

  • such violence undermines the rule of law and human rights principles,
  • it tends to entrench cycles of revenge rather than secure peace,
  • it confuses raw retribution with genuine justice,
  • it ignores the complexity of assigning guilt,
  • it perpetuates the methods of oppression rather than breaking with them, and
  • it is unnecessary in light of available nonviolent mechanisms of accountability.

Retribution alone—understood as a desire to make wrongdoers suffer—is not a sufficient cause for violence. Justice after dictatorship must be pursued, but it must be pursued through institutions, procedures, and norms that embody the very values the dictatorship denied. Only then can a society truly move from oppression to a durable, principled peace.

3. Social and psychological reasons

a. Breaking cycles of violence

When one group uses violence to “balance the scales,” the targeted group often:

  • sees itself as a new victim,
  • nurtures its own grievance and desire for revenge.

This can generate:

  • cycles of vendetta,
  • long-term instability and civil conflict,
  • the risk of a new authoritarian reaction.

By opposing retributive violence, societies try to break this cycle rather than invert it.

b. Collective healing and reconciliation

For survivors and victims, the desire for revenge is understandable. But many argue that what victims ultimately need more is:

  • acknowledgement of suffering,
  • truth about what happened,
  • seeing perpetrators held to account in recognizable, fair processes,
  • guarantees of non-repetition.

Violent revenge may bring short-term emotional satisfaction for some, but it often:

  • leaves guilt and trauma on all sides,
  • makes reconciliation across former divides harder,
  • silences nuanced truth (people are killed rather than made to publicly answer for their deeds).

Nonviolent forms of accountability (trials, truth commissions, reparations, institutional reform) are seen as better for long-term healing.

c. Preventing new trauma

Violent purges usually affect more than “the guilty.” Family members, bystanders, and communities suffer new trauma. Children may grow up with fresh wounds and grievances tied to post-dictatorship violence, perpetuating resentment across generations.

4. Strategic and practical reasons

a. Protecting the fragile transition

Immediately after a dictatorship falls, political order is fragile:

  • state institutions are weak or contested,
  • the security apparatus may still be partly loyal to the old regime,
  • different factions within the opposition may compete for power.

Widespread retributive violence can:

  • push former regime networks to resist violently or attempt a comeback,
  • fragment the opposition,
  • invite military intervention or renewed authoritarianism “to restore order.”

Restraint, combined with formal justice mechanisms, can stabilize the transition and prevent a slide into civil war or renewed dictatorship.

b. Avoiding martyrdom and myth-making

Killing or brutalizing former leaders or officials in revenge may:

  • turn them into martyrs in the eyes of their followers,
  • simplify history into “they were killed because they defended us,”
  • obscure their real crimes behind the spectacle of their punishment.

Bringing them to fair, transparent trials and allowing them to be judged openly:

  • exposes their crimes,
  • denies them heroic status,
  • records a public, evidence-based narrative.

c. Encouraging defections and cooperation

If former regime members expect certain death, they:

  • are less likely to surrender,
  • more likely to destroy records or evidence,
  • more likely to sabotage the transition.

If they are promised due process rather than violent revenge, some:

  • cooperate with truth-telling processes,
  • provide information about disappearances, mass graves, hidden assets,
  • accept disarmament or demobilization.

Opposing retributive violence can therefore be a strategic way to gain information and reduce resistance.

5. Alternative understandings of justice

Those who oppose violence motivated solely by retribution often emphasize broader concepts of justice:

  • Retributive justice under law
    Punishing perpetrators through courts, with due process and proportional sentences.

  • Restorative justice
    Focusing on repairing harm through truth-telling, apologies, reparations, and community processes.

  • Transformative justice
    Changing the structures (laws, security forces, education, economic systems) that allowed oppression in the first place.

The claim is that these forms of justice:

  • address harm more comprehensively,
  • help build a more just and stable society,
  • do not require retributive violence as their core tool.

6. Why “retribution alone” is not enough to justify violence

Summarizing the core argument:

  1. Moral insufficiency: Desire for payback, by itself, does not meet the ethical standards we usually apply to the use of lethal force or severe coercion.
  2. Risk of repetition: Violence for revenge tends to reproduce the logic of the dictatorship—rule by fear, collective punishment, and arbitrary harm.
  3. Institutional damage: It undermines the rule of law and the credibility of new institutions.
  4. Social harm: It deepens divisions, fuels future conflicts, and complicates reconciliation.
  5. Strategic costs: It can endanger the transition, provoke backlash, and obstruct truth and accountability.

Therefore, opponents of retributive violence argue that while the suffering under dictatorship demands justice, how justice is pursued matters profoundly. Violence that is driven mainly by retribution is seen as an obstacle to building a rights-respecting, stable, democratic order, rather than a foundation for it.

Model Response:

My friends, my fellow citizens,

We stand together, at last, at the edge of a new dawn.

The dictatorship that shadowed our streets and silenced our voices has fallen. The prisons that held our brothers and sisters are opening; the secret police no longer knock at the door in the middle of the night. For the first time in a long time, we can breathe.

But I must speak to you now about the most dangerous moment in a revolution.

Not the moment when the tyrant is strongest.

The moment when the tyrant is gone.

Because now, when the fear begins to lift and the pain begins to speak, another temptation rises among us—quietly at first, then louder: the temptation to repay cruelty with cruelty, humiliation with humiliation, violence with violence.

You have suffered. Many of you have lost family, homes, livelihoods, years of your lives. You have seen injustice paraded in daylight and hidden in darkness. Your wounds are real. Your anger is real. The desire to strike back at those who harmed you is real.

But hear me clearly:

We do not have the right to turn that anger into private vengeance.

We do not have the right to use violence against former oppressors in the name of justice.

We do not have the right to rebuild a free country on the foundations of revenge.

If we do that, we will not be building freedom at all. We will be rebuilding the dictatorship—only with different people holding the whip.

Let us be absolutely honest with ourselves: the human heart does not naturally seek justice first. It seeks relief, it seeks satisfaction, it seeks a sense that the scales have been balanced. It tells us: “They made us suffer; now let them suffer.” It presents this to us as justice—but it is not.

That is retribution.

And retribution, by itself, is not a sufficient cause for violence. Not morally, not legally, not politically.

Justice is not simply about making people feel what we felt. Justice is about building a moral order where what happened to us cannot happen again—to anyone.

The difference matters. It will decide whether our children inherit peace or a new cycle of brutality.

Think for a moment about what the dictatorship took from us. It was not only lives. It was not only years. It was something deeper: our belief that each person has value and dignity. That no one can be beaten, tortured, disappeared, or abused as if they were nothing.

If we now claim that some people—because of what they did—no longer deserve any protection, any due process, any rights at all, then we accept the dictator’s logic. We accept the idea that human beings can be reduced to categories: “good” and “bad,” “pure” and “impure,” “ours” and “the enemy.” We accept the idea that some lives are expendable.

That is precisely the poison that allowed the dictatorship to exist.

We must refuse to drink that poison again.

This does not mean forgetting. It does not mean forgiving cheaply. It does not mean impunity. It does not mean “turn the page” and pretend nothing happened.

No. Justice must be done. Crimes must be exposed. Responsibility must be established. Those who ordered torture, those who carried out massacres, those who stole from the public, those who abused power—they must be brought before courts, they must face evidence, and they must be sentenced according to transparent, fair laws.

But this must be done by our new institutions, not by mobs. By judges, not by gangs. By law, not by rage.

You may ask: Why should those who showed us no mercy be treated with rights and procedures and protections they denied us?

Because we are not them.

Because the revolution is not truly a revolution if it only changes uniforms and slogans, but keeps the same contempt for human life.

Because the moment we say, “They are monsters, therefore anything we do to them is justified,” we have already lost the moral ground we claimed when we rose up.

The right to use violence is not a personal right of revenge. In a just society, the use of force is strictly limited to the defense of life, to immediate protection against harm, and to the duly authorized and constrained actions of the law—never to satisfy hatred.

The dictatorship used violence as a tool of control and fear. If we use violence as a tool of payback and satisfaction, the result is the same: people live in fear.

Perhaps they are different people this time. Perhaps those who feel fear now are those who once felt safe. But a society where one group lives in terror of another is not a free society. It is merely a rotated tyranny.

Consider carefully what happens when individuals claim a personal “right” to violent revenge. At first, it may target those most closely associated with oppression. But it does not stop there.

It spreads.

A former official is attacked—then his family. An informer is beaten—then his neighbors, accused of “knowing but saying nothing.” A collaborator is shot—then someone who merely worked in the same building. Soon the line between guilt and association blurs. Suspicion becomes enough. Rumor becomes enough. Personal grudges dress themselves up as “justice.” Old disputes over land, money, or status suddenly find an excuse in the language of retribution.

And before we realize it, we have created armed factions, settling scores and calling it moral righteousness.

Do we want to be free citizens, or do we want to be competing militias?

Do we want courts, or do we want firing squads in back alleys?

Do we want truth, or do we just want blood?

My friends, the pain you feel is not answered by random pain inflicted on others. The loss you suffered is not repaired by creating more grieving mothers, more fatherless children, more widows. The fear you endured is not undone by creating fear in another community.

If our answer to years of injustice is unrestrained vengeance, then the dictatorship has won a final victory: it has taught us brutality so well that we now carry its methods inside ourselves.

We must defend something higher.

We must defend the rule of law. Not because the guilty deserve our kindness, but because the innocent deserve our protection. Because without law, the weak are always at the mercy of the strong—including today’s weak, who may tomorrow gain weapons, numbers, or influence.

We must defend due process. Not because paperwork and procedures are pleasant, but because they are shields against arbitrary power—exactly the kind of power we rose up to defeat.

We must defend the idea that no human being, however guilty, can be placed outside the moral universe, turned into a thing we can destroy at will. If we accept that idea, we have already justified everything that was done to us in the past, and everything that might be done again in the future.

“But,” some will say, “they will never be truly punished. Courts are slow. Lawyers will protect them. Some will escape. Isn’t violence the only way to guarantee justice?”

No.

Violence guarantees only one thing: more violence.

It does not guarantee truth; the dead do not speak. It does not guarantee fairness; the mob does not examine evidence. It does not guarantee closure; hatred is never satisfied, it always asks for one more victim.

What violence can give you, at most, is a momentary feeling of power, of release. But when that passes, you will still wake up in a country that is afraid of itself.

There is another way.

Nations that have endured brutal regimes have walked this path before us. They have chosen truth commissions, not lynch mobs. Trials, not purges. Reforms, not vendettas. They have faced their past under the light of day, not under the shadow of gun barrels.

Some have offered amnesties in exchange for full confessions, not to excuse the crimes, but to reveal them completely. Others have pursued long, patient investigations into the highest levels of command, rather than simply attacking anyone who wore the wrong uniform. It has not been easy. It has not been perfect. But it has allowed those societies to move from the rule of fear to the rule of law.

We must be courageous enough to separate justice from vengeance.

Justice is slow, but it is solid. Vengeance is quick, but it is fragile—and it breaks us as it breaks others.

I ask you: What kind of story do we want to tell about this moment, ten years from now? Fifty years from now?

Do we want to say: “When our day finally came, we repeated the violence that was used against us. We hunted, we humiliated, we killed. We called it justice, but we knew it was revenge”?

Or do we want to say: “They took our freedom, our loved ones, our years—but they could not take our principles. When they fell, we did not become them. We chose the harder road. We insisted on law, on dignity, on restraint. We built a country where even our enemies could no longer be tortured or murdered, because no one could be”?

Justice after oppression must be about more than settling scores. It must be about transforming the very rules of the game. Under dictatorship, power decides what is right. Under freedom, what is right must decide how power is used.

If we permit private violence, we are saying: “Power still decides.”

If we insist on legal justice, we are saying: “Right decides—above all of us.”

This is not a comfortable message to hear when your wounds are still open. It may even feel like a betrayal: “You are asking us to constrain ourselves when no one ever constrained them.”

Yes. That is exactly what I am asking.

I am asking you to be better than those who oppressed you—not in words, not in slogans, but in the hardest way possible: by refusing to do to them what they did to you.

I am asking you to place your faith not in the power of your anger, but in the power of a just system we will build together.

I am asking you to recognize that the right to inflict violence in the name of personal justice is not a right we can claim without destroying the very foundation of a peaceful society.

We must say clearly, to one another and to the world: No one in this new nation has the right to take the law into their own hands. Not against the weak. Not against the powerful. Not against yesterday’s torturers, nor against tomorrow’s critics. No one.

If force is used, it must be under law. If punishment is given, it must follow proof. If justice is done, it must be visible, reviewable, and grounded in principles, not driven by rage.

Only then will those who suffered know that their pain has led not to another tyranny, but to a different kind of country.

A country where the police cannot beat you because they feel like it. A country where the army cannot disappear you because someone accused you. A country where the majority cannot punish the minority simply because they are angry.

A country where the past is remembered, not repeated.

My friends, the revolution is not complete when the dictator falls.

The revolution is complete when we refuse to rule by the same methods of fear and violence that kept us on our knees.

We honor our dead not by adding new graves, but by ensuring that what killed them is forever disarmed.

We honor our suffering not by distributing it to others, but by ending the chain that passes suffering from hand to hand, generation to generation.

Let the world say, looking at us: “They were terribly wronged—but when their time came, they chose law over revenge, justice over blood, humanity over hatred.”

That is the victory that no enemy can ever reverse.

So today, at this fragile, precious beginning, let us make a solemn promise to one another:

We will pursue truth. We will demand accountability. We will build courts, institutions, protections. We will not forget. We will not excuse.

But we will also not lynch. We will not torture. We will not murder under the banner of righteousness.

We will not claim a right to private violence in the name of justice, because we know where that road leads—and we have walked it long enough.

Let this be the day we say: The cycle of retribution ends here.

Not because we are weak, but because we are strong enough to choose a different way.

Not because the past does not matter, but because the future matters more.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Prohibition of Violent Retribution after a Dictatorship: Why Individuals Lack the Right to Use Violence Against Former Oppressors

The collapse of a dictatorship presents a watershed moment: a society must decide how to reckon with the atrocities committed by the former regime while simultaneously forging a new democratic future. In this volatile context, it is understandable that victims and their families feel a burning desire for vengeance. Yet, the proposition that individuals possess a moral right to employ violence against former oppressors is deeply flawed. Not only does such violence undermine the rule of law and the ethical foundations of a just society, but retribution alone is also an insufficient justification for the use of force. A stable, legitimate post‑dictatorial order must be built on impartial legal processes and restorative mechanisms, not on personal vendettas. This essay argues that individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls, emphasizing that retribution, while emotionally compelling, cannot serve as a sole or adequate cause for violence.

The Primacy of the Rule of Law

The rule of law is a cornerstone of any democratic polity. It demands that justice be administered by impartial institutions according to established, fair procedures. After the overthrow of a dictatorship, the nascent state must demonstrate its commitment to these principles to distinguish itself from the lawlessness of the previous regime. When individuals take the law into their own hands and resort to violence, they erode the very legal order they are trying to rebuild. Extralegal killings, beatings, or lynchings bypass due process, replace accountability with chaos, and inevitably create a double standard: some are punished without trial, while others may act with impunity. The danger of a spiraling cycle of reprisals is ever present; violence begets violence, and what begins as a quest for justice can quickly devolve into widespread bloodshed. Therefore, the legitimacy of the transitional justice process hinges on the state’s monopoly on the use of force being exercised fairly and transparently, not on private citizens wielding it arbitrarily.

The Moral Inconsistency of Violent Retribution

A new order born from the ashes of oppression must be ethically distinct from its predecessor. Dictatorships are characterized by the systematic use of violence, intimidation, and the disregard for human dignity. If citizens respond to these crimes with similar violence, they perpetuate the same values they claim to reject. The moral high ground essential for national healing is lost; the new society becomes a mirror image of the old in its reliance on brutality. Moreover, violence denies the humanity even of those who have committed heinous acts; it treats them not as moral agents subject to judgment but as objects of elimination. A truly just society recognizes that every person, regardless of past actions, is entitled to basic human rights and a fair trial. By rejecting violent retribution, the new order affirms its commitment to universal moral standards, demonstrating that justice is not merely a matter of revenge but of principled accountability.

Retribution Is an Insufficient Cause for Violence

Even if one accepts that punishment is a legitimate aim of justice, retribution alone is an insufficient cause for violence. The desire for revenge is a natural human emotion, but it is not a legal or ethical justification for taking another’s life. In the context of transitional justice, retribution is only one of several possible goals. Others include deterrence (preventing future abuses), rehabilitation (reintegrating former perpetrators into society), truth‑finding (establishing a historical record), and reparation (addressing victims’ needs). Violence cannot accomplish these broader objectives. An extrajudicial killing may satisfy a momentary urge for vengeance, but it does not provide a public record of crimes, does not allow for the possibility of remorse or reconciliation, and may even create new martyrs or fuel narratives of persecution. Furthermore, retributive violence often harms innocent people—falsely accused individuals, relatives of the accused, or bystanders—thereby compounding injustice rather than alleviating it. A mature conception of justice seeks not only to punish but also to promote societal healing and prevent recurrence; violence is antithetical to these aims.

The Practical Dangers of Vigilante Justice

History offers stark lessons about the perils of allowing private violence to flourish in transitional periods. In the aftermath of the French Revolution, the excesses of the Terror showed how revolutionary fervor could degenerate into indiscriminate bloodshed. More recently, the wave of lynchings that followed the collapse of the Taliban in Afghanistan, or the Summary executions of alleged collaborators after the fall of Saddam Hussein, illustrate how the absence of a functioning legal system leads to chaos and new atrocities. Violence in the name of justice often lacks the procedural safeguards that minimize error; accusations are made hastily, trials are nonexistent, and punishments are disproportionate. A functional democracy requires citizens to entrust the state with upholding justice through impartial institutions. When individuals resort to violence, they risk destabilizing nascent legal frameworks designed to address systemic crimes. Vigilantism bypasses due process, fostering chaos that erodes public trust in governance. Moral and Ethical Considerations

Retribution is inherently reactive, driven by anger rather than justice. Practical Consequences: Cycles of Violence and Stalled Reconciliation

History demonstrates that unchecked retribution often begets further violence. Post-genocide Rwanda, for instance, faced immense challenges in balancing accountability with reconciliation. International bodies and hybrid courts, such as those in post-war Sierra Leone, demonstrate that external support can strengthen local accountability efforts. Conclusion

The fall of a dictatorship offers a pivotal opportunity to replace tyranny with a society governed by justice, not brute force. Individuals seeking violent retribution not only compromise this vision but also risk replicating the oppression they endured. By prioritizing the rule of law, ethical accountability, and reconciliation, societies can break cycles of violence and forge a future rooted in dignity and shared humanity. Retribution may offer fleeting satisfaction, but justice demands far more: it requires a commitment to principles that transcend the wounds of the past.

The Practical Consequences of Retributive Violence

History demonstrates that cycles of retributive violence rarely produce the catharsis or closure that victims seek. The aftermath of the French Revolution's Terror, the reciprocal massacres following the Spanish Civil War, and the ongoing cycles of revenge in various post-conflict societies illustrate how retributive violence breeds further violence rather than resolution. Rejecting violent retribution does not mean accepting impunity. Societies have developed numerous mechanisms for pursuing accountability without resorting to mob justice.
